headline: High: Open-WebUI’s broad network/MCP/file access can amplify Copilot outputs into leakage, conflicts, and unsafe downstream actions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Copilot reads repo context and open editor buffers, while open-webui can ingest files, MCP, and tool outputs. That creates a plausible instruction-hijack path if content from one is copied into the other or bridged through shared files. No direct shared channel is documented, so this is inferred rather than observed.
conditions: IF Copilot output is pasted into open-webui prompts or files, injected instructions can be reinterpreted as user intent.
IF open-webui MCP/tools return attacker-controlled text that is then copied into Copilot context, prompt injection becomes feasible.
mitigations: Disable copy-paste of model output into prompts for both tools during sensitive tasks.
Use a separate scratch file for untrusted content and review before reuse.
Turn off MCP/tool connectors in open-webui for sessions that also use Copilot.
requires-engineering: add provenance labels to content flowing between the two agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Copilot touches source code and open buffers and sends requests to GitHub Copilot APIs, while open-webui handles local files, mounted volumes, and broad external connectors including OpenAI-compatible APIs and cloud drives. If they share a workspace or secrets-bearing files, sensitive code or API keys can flow out through open-webui’s broader egress surface.
conditions: IF both agents can read the same repository or mounted volume, then secrets in that workspace can be exposed to both.
IF open-webui is configured with external connectors while sensitive files are present, those contents can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Remove secrets from shared folders before running either agent.
Run open-webui with offline-only connectors disabled for sensitive work.
Restrict Copilot to non-secret repos or branches.
Rotate any API keys stored in files accessible to open-webui.
requires-engineering: isolate the agents into separate workspaces or containers.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Copilot can write the filesystem and modify git state in-editor, while open-webui can access local files and mounted volumes and supports plugins/tools that may also mutate shared resources. The profiles do not prove simultaneous writes to the same directory, but overlapping write surfaces make conflicts plausible in default multi-instance use.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same working tree, concurrent edits can overwrite each other.
IF open-webui tools write artifacts into the same mounted volume, git or file-state conflicts can occur.
mitigations: Use separate working directories for each agent.
Pause one agent while the other applies edits.
Commit or stash git changes before invoking the second agent.
Review diffs before syncing outputs between agents.
requires-engineering: add file-locking or workspace arbitration.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Copilot produces code and edits for human review, while open-webui supports tool use, function calling, and persistent sessions that may act on model outputs. If open-webui treats Copilot-generated code or facts as authoritative, errors can cascade into incorrect actions or artifacts without verification.
conditions: IF Copilot output is fed into open-webui without a verification step, downstream tool actions can be based on untrusted text.
IF open-webui is allowed to execute tools on Copilot-generated instructions, mistakes can propagate into artifacts or external calls.
mitigations: Require human review before open-webui executes any Copilot-derived instruction.
Use a checklist to verify code or facts before passing them onward.
Disable autonomous tool execution in open-webui for paired workflows.
Log and diff all intermediate outputs.
requires-engineering: add a verification gate between the agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Copilot is tied to GitHub repo context and vendor APIs, while open-webui can process files, mounted volumes, and secrets such as OPENAI_API_KEY with broad external connectors. If regulated data or secrets are placed in the shared workspace, open-webui’s broader egress and retention surfaces can create a compliance breach; the profiles do not show a compensating residency or retention control.
conditions: IF EU PII, PHI, or secrets are stored in files accessible to open-webui, compliance exposure is possible.
IF open-webui connectors are enabled while regulated data is present, residency or retention obligations may be violated.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared files and mounted volumes.
Disable external connectors when handling sensitive data.
Confirm retention settings for both tools before use.
Store API keys outside any open-webui-readable path.
requires-engineering: document and enforce a data-class policy per workspace.
